title: Chaos Engineering & Fault Injection
summary: Designing on the assumption that your resilience mechanisms will be tested by deliberately breaking things in production, not just reasoned about on a whiteboard.

slides.markdown:
Every mechanism in this group — circuit breakers, retries, bulkheads, load shedding — is a claim about how the system behaves during a failure. **Chaos engineering** tests that claim directly: deliberately inject the failure in a controlled way and see if the mechanism actually does what it's supposed to.

This topic covers the discipline behind doing that safely: defining a steady-state hypothesis, controlling blast radius, what kinds of faults to inject, and how it differs from a scheduled disaster-recovery drill.

slides.sectionTitle: The core idea: you don't know a resilience mechanism works until you've triggered the failure it's for
slides.markdown:
A circuit breaker configured with a threshold and a cooldown, never actually tripped by a real failure, is untested code — it might have a bug in the state transition, a misconfigured threshold, or simply never fire because the failure detection logic is wrong. Code review and unit tests catch some of this, but they test the mechanism in isolation, not against the real, messy failure modes of a live system under load.

Chaos engineering's premise: the only way to know a resilience mechanism actually works is to trigger the real failure condition — kill an instance, inject latency, drop a dependency — and observe whether the system responds the way it's supposed to.

This reframes resilience work: designing a circuit breaker is half the job; proving it trips and recovers correctly under real conditions is the other half, and most teams skip it.

slides.sectionTitle: Steady-state hypothesis: define what "normal" looks like before you break anything
slides.markdown:
Before injecting any fault, define a **steady-state hypothesis**: a measurable statement of what "the system is healthy" looks like — for example, "checkout success rate stays above 99.9% and p99 latency stays under 400ms." This is the baseline the experiment checks against, not a vague sense that "things seem fine."

Without an explicit hypothesis, an experiment can't actually conclude anything — if you inject a fault and eyeball the dashboards, you have no principled way to say whether the system passed or failed, only an impression.

The hypothesis should be specific enough that a teammate with no context could look at the same metrics after the experiment and independently agree whether it held or broke.

slides.markdown:
![Four-step chaos experiment flow with an automatic abort path](assets/chaos-engineering-loop.svg)

The loop is deliberately linear and falsifiable: each experiment either confirms the hypothesis held under the injected fault, or reveals a gap between the assumed and actual resilience — both are useful outcomes, not just the "pass" case.

The abort path is not optional — it's what makes running this safely in production defensible at all, discussed next.

slides.sectionTitle: Blast radius control: starting in staging, then a tiny percentage of production traffic
slides.markdown:
Chaos experiments graduate through increasing blast radius, never jumping straight to "break it in production for everyone." Start in **staging** to catch obvious bugs in the resilience mechanism itself with zero user risk. Move to production but scoped to an **internal or canary** slice of traffic. Then a **small percentage of real production traffic** (often single-digit percent), with the ability to abort instantly.

Each stage should have its own steady-state hypothesis and its own abort criteria — staging passing doesn't guarantee production will, since staging rarely has production's real traffic patterns, data volume, or concurrent incidents.

The blast radius should scale with confidence, not with convenience — jump stages only once the previous stage has actually passed, not because running in staging is slower to set up.

slides.sectionTitle: What to inject: killed instances, added latency, dropped packets, exhausted disk/memory
slides.markdown:
Real fault-injection tools cover a range of failure shapes, each testing a different resilience mechanism. **Killed instances** — terminate a server or container mid-traffic to test failover and load-balancer health checks. **Added latency** — artificially slow a dependency's responses to test timeouts, hedging, and circuit breakers (these react differently to "slow" than to "down"). **Dropped packets / network partitions** — simulate a service becoming unreachable to test retry and fallback logic. **Exhausted disk/memory/CPU** — starve a resource to test backpressure and degradation under real resource pressure, not just simulated errors.

Each fault type exercises a different part of the resilience toolkit — killing instances mostly tests failover, while added latency specifically tests the timeout and circuit-breaker tuning covered elsewhere in this group.

Pick the fault that matches the mechanism you're actually trying to validate, rather than running one generic "break things" test and hoping it covers everything.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: chaos engineering (continuous, deliberate fault injection) vs a DR failover drill (a specific, scheduled scenario)
slides.markdown:
| | Chaos engineering | DR failover drill |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Many small, varied faults, run continuously or frequently | One large, specific scenario — e.g. "primary region goes fully down" |
| Frequency | Ongoing, often automated | Scheduled, periodic (quarterly, annually) |
| Tests | Everyday resilience mechanisms (breakers, retries, bulkheads) | Full disaster-recovery process, RTO/RPO commitments — see RTO/RPO and failover drills |
| Typical output | Confidence in specific, small mechanisms | Confidence in the full recovery runbook end-to-end |

**How to decide:** they're complementary, not substitutes — chaos engineering validates the small mechanisms constantly so the big DR drill isn't the first time anything gets tested; the DR drill validates the parts (full region failover, data recovery) chaos experiments are too broad and disruptive to exercise routinely.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: running a chaos experiment with no automatic abort when it's actually causing user-facing harm
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We're only injecting a small fault, and we're watching the dashboards, so we'll notice and stop it manually if something goes wrong."

**Why it's wrong:** manual monitoring during a live experiment is slower than the harm it's meant to catch — by the time a human notices a metric crossing a bad threshold and manually halts the experiment, real users may have already been affected for minutes, which is exactly the outcome chaos engineering is supposed to avoid causing.

**Correct model:** every experiment needs an automated abort condition wired directly to the same metrics defining the steady-state hypothesis — if error rate or latency crosses a defined safety threshold, the experiment stops itself immediately, with no human in the loop required to notice first.

slides.sectionTitle: The staff-level nuance: chaos engineering tests people and process, not just code
slides.markdown:
The most mature chaos programs don't just verify that a circuit breaker trips — they verify that a human on call would actually notice, diagnose, and respond correctly if it did, in the middle of the night, with the same tools and runbooks they'd have during a real incident. An experiment that silently confirms the breaker worked, without ever paging anyone or exercising the on-call escalation path, has validated the code but left the socio-technical system — dashboards, alert thresholds, runbook accuracy, who gets paged — completely untested.

This is why some organizations run unannounced (to the responding team, though never unbounded in blast radius) chaos experiments during business hours: not to catch the on-call engineer off guard for its own sake, but because a scheduled, expected experiment gets a different, more careful human response than a real 3 AM page would. Netflix's original chaos tooling grew out of exactly this insight — a resilience mechanism nobody has ever watched fire, escalate, and get paged on is unverified in the dimension that actually matters during a real outage.

The senior-level framing: "does the circuit breaker trip correctly" is a code-correctness question; "does the team detect and respond to it tripping" is the harder, more valuable question chaos engineering is also meant to answer.
